title: Pandan Chiffon Cake
changes_from_base: Pandan juice and coconut milk replace the water and vanilla; no extract or colouring needed.
summary: This follows the classic chiffon method, with fresh pandan juice and coconut milk replacing the water and vanilla, giving the cake its natural green colour and fragrance without any extract or colouring.
equipment: 25 cm two-piece tube (angel food) tin, ungreased and unlined
fine sieve and muslin or a clean tea towel
stand mixer or electric hand whisk
wire rack or glass bottle for cooling upside down

ingredients.item: cake flour (or plain flour; see note)
ingredients.note: plain flour works with a slightly firmer crumb

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt
large egg whites, at room temperature
pandan leaves (fresh or frozen), cut into 2 cm pieces

steps.title: Make the Pandan Juice
steps.text: Blitz the pandan leaves with the water until they're broken down to the texture of fine grass clippings, then press the mixture through muslin or a clean tea towel to squeeze out roughly 60ml of vivid green juice.

steps.title: Heat the Oven
steps.text: Preheat the oven to 165°C (145°C fan), allowing at least 20 minutes, and position a shelf in the lower third.

steps.title: Leave the Tin Ungreased
steps.text: Resist greasing or lining the tube tin. The rising batter needs bare metal to hold onto, and that's precisely what lets this cake reach its full towering height.

steps.title: Make the Batter
steps.text: Combine the flour, 150g of the sugar, baking powder and salt in a large bowl. Make a well in the centre and pour in the egg yolks, oil, pandan juice and coconut milk, whisking until the mixture is smooth and glossy, about 1 minute. Here the coconut milk and pandan juice stand in for the vanilla, lending their colour and scent to the batter naturally.

steps.title: Whisk the Meringue
steps.text: On medium speed, whisk the egg whites and cream of tartar until foamy, then slowly sprinkle in the 140g of sugar while whisking on medium-high speed until you reach stiff, glossy peaks that hold straight up. Without a meringue this firm, the cake won't have the structure to climb so tall.

steps.title: Fold Together
steps.text: Stir a third of the meringue into the batter to loosen it, then fold in the rest with a spatula in two additions, making sure to scrape right down to the bottom of the bowl, until the mixture is free of white streaks.

steps.title: Fill and Bake
steps.text: Scrape the batter into the tin, pass a skewer through it to burst any large bubbles, and even out the top. Bake for 50-60 minutes, until it has risen well and the top is golden over the green crumb and springs back when touched; the cracks should look dry and a skewer should come out clean.

steps.title: Cool Upside Down
steps.text: As soon as it's out of the oven, invert the tin onto its feet, or balance it over the neck of a bottle, and leave it to cool completely, about 2 hours. This upside-down cooling keeps the warm, fragile sponge from caving in before it sets.

steps.title: Unmould
steps.text: Trace a thin knife around the edges of the tin and around the central tube, remove the base, then free the cake from the bottom. Finish with a dusting of icing sugar or a spoonful of whipped cream.

tips: Squeeze the pandan leaves thoroughly - a weak juice gives a pale cake with very little flavour.
Never grease the tin - a greased tin is the single biggest reason chiffon cakes slide back down as they cool.
Whisk the meringue to stiff, not soft, peaks; a soft meringue won't hold the cake's height.
Cool it upside down straight after baking to keep the delicate crumb from collapsing.
Don't taste the raw dough or batter: raw flour and raw egg aren't safe to eat until baked.
storage: Keep covered at room temperature for up to 3 days, or in the fridge for up to 5 days. It freezes well, wrapped tightly, for up to 2 months; thaw at room temperature before serving.
